title: Tourist killed after two helicopters collide in Nepal's Everest region - Times of Malta
description: Tourist killed after two helicopters collide in Nepal's Everest region  Times of Malta
publisher.title: Times of Malta
full_article:
An Indian tourist was killed and a New Zealand national injured when two helicopters collided and crashed while attempting to land in Nepal's Everest region on Tuesday, police told AFP.

Small helicopters are widely used in the Himalayan nation to transport tourists, climbers and supplies, as well as to carry out emergency evacuations.

The country's challenging terrain and rapidly changing weather conditions make aviation operations particularly hazardous.

The small helicopters operated by Fishtail Air and Air Dynasty crashed into each other as both came into land on a snowy site in Solukhumbu district on Tuesday morning.

"The 47-year-old Indian tourist died on the spot," Nabin Raja Budhathoki, in charge of Solukhumbu District Police, told AFP.

"The injured 53-year-old citizen... from New Zealand has been airlifted to Kathmandu for further treatment," he added.

Arrangements were also being made to airlift the body of the deceased to the capital Kathmandu.

Both of the pilots survived the accident.

Nepal is home to eight of the world's 14 highest mountains, including Everest, and attracts thousands of foreign climbers and trekkers every year.

Set along a picturesque bend of the Rapti River, with uninterrupted views of the surrounding forests and hills, the 22-room-and-suite luxury retreat adjoins the buffer zone of Chitwan National Park, one of South Asia’s most significant wildlife destinations. The opening marks the brand’s expansion into its fourth country, following India, Bhutan and Sri Lanka.

description: Indian killed in Nepal helicopter collision amid global developments  India Today
publisher.title: India Today
full_article:
An Indian national was killed in a helicopter collision in Nepal on Tuesday, while political, diplomatic, legal and security developments were reported from several countries, according to news agency Press Trust of India.

The developments included voting in the United States mid-term elections, National Security Adviser Ajit Doval's meeting with Vietnam's president, Indian Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri's planned visit to Nepal, court proceedings in Sri Lanka, an arrest in the Maldives, an attack on a polio team in Pakistan and the continuing Russia-Ukraine war.

A 47-year-old Indian national was killed and another passenger was injured when two helicopters collided while landing in Nepal's Solukhumbu district, police told PTI.

Americans were voting in the mid-term elections on Tuesday. The polls are widely being seen as a referendum on Donald Trump's presidency, which has been marked by a prolonged war in Iran, rising inflation, trade wars and deep divisions in society.

title: Vikram Misri heads to Nepal to prepare Balendra Shah's India visit - India Today
description: Vikram Misri heads to Nepal to prepare Balendra Shah's India visit  India Today
publisher.title: India Today
full_article:
Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri will begin a two-day visit to Nepal on Wednesday, November 4, with discussions expected to focus on reviewing bilateral ties and preparing for Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah's likely visit to India later this month.

Shah is likely to visit India in the last week of November in what would be his first bilateral trip since assuming office in March, according to Nepal's Foreign Ministry sources quoted by news agency PTI. The dates of the proposed visit have not yet been officially announced.

advertisement ❮❯

Read Full Story

Misri will visit Nepal from November 4 to 5 at the invitation of his Nepali counterpart, Amrit Bahadur Rai, Nepal's Foreign Ministry said in a statement.

During the visit, the two foreign secretaries will hold bilateral talks and review the entire range of Nepal-India relations. They will also exchange views on matters of mutual interest and discuss ways to further strengthen the close and long-standing ties between the two countries, the ministry said.

Nepal holds strategic importance for India, with the two countries sharing longstanding historical and cultural ties, often described by their leaders as the age-old "Roti Beti" relationship.

The landlocked Himalayan nation depends heavily on India for the movement of goods and services. Its access to the sea is through India, while most of its requirements are imported from or through the neighbouring country.

However, bilateral ties witnessed some unease in May after Shah called for China and the United Kingdom to be involved in resolving the long-standing border dispute between India and Nepal.

New Delhi rejected any role for third parties in addressing the dispute, maintaining that the two countries have an established bilateral mechanism to resolve all aspects of the boundary issue.

India and Nepal have a longstanding territorial dispute over Lipulekh, Limpiyadhura and Kalapani. India has consistently maintained that these territories are part of Uttarakhand.

description: Nonresident Nepali Citizens Can Get Free Two-Year Residence Visas, but Many Don’t Know It  nepyork
publisher.title: nepyork
full_article:
KATHMANDU, Nepal — For decades, Nepalis living abroad have campaigned for a principle they often express as “Once a Nepali, always a Nepali.” At the center of that effort has been the demand to preserve their connection to Nepal, including greater recognition of their rights after acquiring foreign citizenship.

Under Nepal’s previous citizenship law, Nepali citizens automatically lost their Nepali citizenship after acquiring citizenship in another country. As a result, people of Nepali origin who became foreign citizens faced legal and administrative hurdles in their country of birth. Those obstacles affected everything from purchasing property and claiming inheritance to conducting financial transactions, operating businesses and traveling to and from Nepal.

To address some of these concerns, Nepal’s Constitution of 2015 introduced a provision for nonresident Nepali citizenship under Article 14.

The provision allows people who previously held Nepali citizenship — or whose parents or grandparents were Nepali citizens — and who later acquired foreign citizenship in countries outside the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation, or SAARC, to obtain nonresident Nepali citizenship. The status is intended to provide economic, social and cultural rights, though it does not grant political rights.

After years of legal and administrative delays, the government began distributing nonresident Nepali citizenship through district administration offices following amendments to the Nepal Citizenship Act of 2006 and its regulations.

But obtaining the citizenship did not immediately eliminate immigration-related complications. Differences between immigration laws and the Non-Resident Nepali Act of 2008 meant that many nonresident Nepalis continued to face visa requirements and fees when visiting or staying in Nepal.

The Department of Immigration began issuing free visas to foreign nationals holding nonresident Nepali citizenship on Jan. 12, 2025. The arrangement received a clearer statutory foundation through amendments to the Non-Resident Nepali Act under the Good Governance Promotion and Public Service Delivery Act, 2025, which took effect on March 31, 2025.

The international arrivals terminal at Tribhuvan International Airport in Kathmandu, Nepal.

A Free Visa for Up to 10 Years, and a Two-Year Residence Visa

Before the amendment, the law allowed foreign citizens of Nepali origin and eligible family members to receive nonresident Nepali visas for periods of up to 10 years. But it did not explicitly guarantee that the visas would be free, nor did it establish a separate two-year residence visa for people holding nonresident Nepali citizenship.

The 2025 amendment clarified and expanded those benefits.

Under Section 11(1) of the amended law, nonresident Nepali citizens, foreign nationals of Nepali origin holding nonresident Nepali identity cards, and their family members are eligible for free nonresident Nepali visas for up to 10 years.

Section 11(1a) provides a separate benefit: Foreign nationals holding nonresident Nepali citizenship can receive a free residence visa valid for two years at a time, with multiple-entry privileges.

Section 11(2) allows the validity of visas issued under Section 11(1) to be extended as necessary. The amended law also explicitly includes holders of nonresident Nepali citizenship in its definition of nonresident Nepalis.

The distinction between the two visa categories is important. The 10-year provision covers a broader group of eligible nonresident Nepalis and their families, while the two-year residence visa specifically applies to people holding nonresident Nepali citizenship.

Applications for Nonresident Nepali Visas Have Increased

Data obtained from the Department of Immigration show a steady increase in the number of people receiving nonresident Nepali visas in recent years, including principal applicants and their dependent family members.

In 2020, the department recorded 509 recipients: 502 principal applicants and seven dependents.

The total increased to 1,482 in 2021, including 1,407 principal applicants and 75 dependents. In 2022, the number reached 2,329, comprising 2,189 principal applicants and 140 dependents.

In 2023, a total of 2,498 people received the visas, including 2,314 principal applicants and 184 dependents. The number rose to 2,664 in 2024, with 2,449 principal applicants and 215 dependents.

The department recorded 3,460 recipients in 2025, including 3,258 principal applicants and 202 dependents.

The latest figures for 2026 show 3,080 recipients: 2,835 principal applicants and 245 dependents.

Savings and Easier Travel to Nepal

The amended provisions offer both financial and practical benefits to eligible nonresident Nepalis.

The removal of visa fees eliminates a recurring expense for people who previously had to pay for residence visas. The two-year multiple-entry provision also allows citizenship holders to travel in and out of Nepal without having to obtain a new visa for each visit during the visa’s validity period.

The arrangement is particularly useful for people who maintain family, property or business ties in Nepal but live permanently in another country. It gives them greater flexibility to spend extended periods in their country of origin and return abroad when necessary.

Despite the benefits, many nonresident Nepali citizenship holders remain unaware of the provision and how to apply for the free residence visa.

How to Apply for the Free Two-Year Visa

Applicants generally need to prepare their nonresident Nepali citizenship certificate, a valid foreign passport and a passport-size photograph. Those applying for eligible family members may also need documents establishing their relationship.

Applicants must then visit the Department of Immigration’s online portal and select the appropriate visa category to complete the application.

After submitting the form, they must present the resulting confirmation and required original documents to the Department of Immigration or the relevant immigration office for verification.

Once the documents have been verified, immigration officials can issue a free, two-year residence visa with multiple-entry privileges under Section 11(1a) of the Non-Resident Nepali Act.

A Department of Immigration official issues a visa sticker in Nepal. Photo: Deependra Dhungana

Broader Rights Remain Unresolved

Although the free visa provision represents a significant benefit, nonresident Nepalis say the broader question of their rights remains unresolved.

Many have continued to call on the government to fully implement the constitutional provisions on nonresident Nepali citizenship and ensure the economic, social and cultural rights promised under the law.

The Constitution provides for those rights, but implementation has been uneven. Some provisions still require additional legislation or regulations, while administrative hurdles continue to limit the practical exercise of existing rights.

For many members of the Nepali diaspora, the free two-year residence visa is an important step toward maintaining closer ties with their homeland. But they say it is only one part of a larger effort to ensure that acquiring foreign citizenship does not sever their legal and practical connection to Nepal.
